577.dq: The phonological word in Nakanai is a rhythmic segment with nuclear stress on the penultimate syllable, and bounded by juncture. [...] Stress consists mainly of increased intensity on the penultimate syllable of each separate word. On the nuclear syllable of a pause group intensity and intonation peak simultaneously on the penultimate syllable of the final word.
577.dloc: Johnston 1980 (PL B-70), App. A4 p.256; sect. 6.3 p.180
577.prule: Primary stress (the nucleus, cued by primary pitch) on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; the word-initial syllable carries primary intensity as a juncture cue; at phrase level the intonation peak falls on the penult of the last word of the pause group. Exceptions: with the intensifier -o stress remains static (no shift to the new penult); with the deictic particles -e/-o it either remains static or shifts to the final syllable; a small group of final-stressed words (tio, io, clipped isa); ten unstressed monosyllabic function words (la, e, te, me, o, le, ga, ge, so, ka).
577.srule: Not mentioned in Johnston 1980 (sect. 1.2.6 p. 22, 3.1.2 pp. 67-70, 6.3 p. 180, App. A1-A4 pp. 247-260 read): no secondary or rhythmic stress is described; the only other word-level prominence noted is 'primary intensity' on the first syllable of every phonological word, treated as a juncture cue, not as stress (A4.1.1-A4.1.2, p. 256).

tn.quote: As mentioned in §2, Sena does not have tones, but rather stress or accent associated to the penultimate syllable of phrasal domains, and realized through phonetic properties such as loudness and higher pitch. Amidst this predictable stress system, it is interesting to observe that ideophones have a special prosody which makes the distinction between high tones (H), indicated with an acute accent, and zero tones (Ø). … The tone position in an ideophone does not depend on phonological rules; it is largely unpredictable and must be learnt for each ideophone. … Ideophonic tones can be contrastive

tn.quote: Når Óláfr meiner at skalden hev bytt um dei elles likelydande ordi bæ-num, dat.sg. b.f. av bær ‘bø, gard’, og bæn-um, dat.pl. ub.f. av bæn f. ‘bøn’, kann det ikkje tydast ut på onnor vis enn at desse tvo ordi var fonologisk ulike. Den einaste måten dei kann ha vore det på, er gjenom tonelag, og ein skilnad 1bæ-num mot 2bæn-um er di meir det me skulde venta ut frå skandinaviske reglar for skifting av dei tvo tonelagi. … tvingar den slutningi seg fram at gamalislendsk hev havt tonelagsskilnad til liks med dei fastlandsnordiske måli.
tn.translation: When Óláfr holds that the skald swapped the otherwise identical-sounding words bæ-num, dat.sg. def. of bær 'farm', and bæn-um, dat.pl. indef. of bæn f. 'prayer', it can only be interpreted as meaning that these two words were phonologically different. The only way they can have been so is through tone accent, and a distinction 1bæ-num vs 2bæn-um is moreover what we should expect from Scandinavian rules for the distribution of the two tone accents. … the conclusion forces itself that Old Icelandic had a tone-accent distinction just like the Mainland Nordic languages.
tn.cite: Myrvoll, Klaus Johan & Trygve Skomedal. 2010. Tonelagsskilnad i islendsk i Tridje grammatiske avhandling. Maal og Minne 102(1): 68-97. Oslo: Novus.
tn.locator: p. 94, section 'Slutning'; accent names 'einstavings og tvostavings tonelag eller tonem 1 og 2' in Innleiding p. 68
tn.note: Argued from the 13th-c. Third Grammatical Treatise to have had the Scandinavian two-way tonal word accent (toneme 1 vs 2), e.g. 1bænum vs 2bænum; no such contrast survives in modern Icelandic.

583.prule: CONFLICT. Paula 2004: always word-final, incl. after affixation ([mɨhi'hu]); compounds final, secondary on 1st member. Garcia 2002: final syllable of the lexical base; affixes never attract stress ([ʃa'raxʊ] /ʃaɾa-xu/, [a'jatʊ]). Souza 2013: moraic iambs L-to-R, primary on rightmost complete foot: light 01 010 0101 ([ka.'ɾa.ta], [nu.ˌwɨ.ta.'pa]); heavy (Vː, glide coda) stressed (['jãː.tã] vs [jã.'tã]).

585.dq: Abkhaz is characterized by strong dynamic stress, which can fall on any syllable in polysyllabic words. ... Stress distinguishes many otherwise homophonic words and word-forms
585.heavy: none: no syllable-weight criterion is mentioned; stress placement is attributed to lexically assigned prosodic valences (dominant/recessive) of syllables/morphemes, not to vowel length or syllable closure (the vowel system is /a/ vs /ə/; surface 'long aa' is analysed as /ħa/, sec. 1.2.1)
585.dflt: not applicable (no weight criterion); source gives no default position
585.prule: Free (lexically contrastive) dynamic stress that 'can fall on any syllable in polysyllabic words'; minimal pairs and triplets by stress position; position determined by the combination of lexically specified valences (dominant/recessive) of the word-form's syllables (Dybo's rule, Spruit 1986).
585.srule: Secondary stress exists (Chirikba 2003: 21 'Longer words can have a secondary stress. Less usually, two syllables in a long word can be equally stressed.'; no placement there). Placement per Andersson 2024 (following Spruit 1986: 73-75): every accented morpheme not immediately followed by an accent is stressed; the leftmost such accent takes primary stress and any others take secondary stress (e.g. [á-sas-ɡʲə̀] 'a guest also', [á-χ-ɥə̀-k'] 'the three people'); placement is lexical/morphemic, not rhythmic, and is acoustically measurable only for some speakers.

tn.quote: The evolution of the Abkhazo-Adyg tonal system may consequently be presented in the following way: Stage 1. Existence of tonal oppositions relevant for every syllable. ... At the end of this stage a system develops, in which tonal oppositions become relevant only on the stressed syllable, but are already neutralised in other syllables. Such a system is to be seen in the Abaza language. Stage 3. The final loss of tonal oppositions, thus giving rise to a "pure" system of paradigmatic accent. Such a system is characteristic for Abkhazian and, to judge from descriptions and texts, for Oubykh.

variants.name: Kalibo Aklanon
variants.prule: Main stress on one of the last two syllables; penult vs final is arbitrary lexical categorization of the root (minimal pairs pitú 'seven' / pítu 'whistle', sugúd 'room' / súgud 'lice comb'); overriding regularity: a word with a closed (CVC) penult always has penultimate stress. Derived words usually copy the root's stress class; some affixes impose their own pattern.
variants.quote: The syllable structure of Aklan is quite simple: only CV and CVC are permitted, aside from certain loan words, and there is no distinction of vowel length. ... Main stress always falls on one of the last two syllables of the word, determined in large part by arbitrary lexical categorization of the root. We thus find roots that are distinguished solely by stress: pitú "seven" pítu "whistle" ... we could suppose that Aklan has two main stress rules, assigning either penultimate or final stress, depending on a diacritic marking attached to the root of the word. Other facts, however, show that matters cannot be this simple. To see this, note that words which have a closed penultimate syllable always bear penultimate stress. ... when suffixes are added to closed-penult roots, the resulting derivatives fall into the ordinary two categories of penultimate and final stress ... We can infer from this that the closed-penult roots, just like other roots, freely bear either diacritic marking for which stress pattern they take; but that when they occur alone, a more general requirement that closed-penult words must have penultimate stress overrides the lexical marking. (Hayes 1980:36-39) || Zorc & de la Cruz 1968:30-31: stress can also be a phoneme, or significant and meaningful sound, in the Aklanon dialect ... The fact that stress is phonemic in these cases should be obvious.

591.heavy: Main-tone placement (GKC 29a): syllable closure - 'a closed penultima can only have the tone if the ultima is open..., whilst a closed ultima can as a rule only be without the tone if the penultima is open'. Tone retraction (GKC 29e-g, fn. 2): three-way - the penult that receives the retracted tone must be 'an open syllable (with a long vowel; but see g)' (retraction onto a closed short-vowel penult is 'anomalous', 29g); the ultima that loses the tone 'must be either an open syllable with a long vowel... or a closed syllable with a short vowel', and 'an unchangeable vowel in a closed final syllable cannot lose the tone' (fn. 2) = superheavy CVVC outranks CVV and CVC. Khan 2020 I.2.3.2 (p. 279): 'An open syllable with a long vowel (CV̄) can be considered to have the same weight as a closed syllable with a short vowel (CVC)... both types of syllable are termed bimoraic'; p. 290: 'a closed syllable with a long vowel (CV̄C) would have three morae' (constraint against superheavy syllables); pp. 292-294: nesiga 'most regularly occurs when the first word ends in an open syllable or else a closed syllable that contains a vowel phoneme without a length specification'. Secondary stress (Khan p. 458; Hayes 1981:87 via StressTyp2): long vowel in an open syllable.
591.dflt: final syllable on the surface per GKC ('as a rule on the final syllable', e.g. qaTAL, daVAR, davaRO with open stressed ultima); Hayes/StressTyp2 underlying analysis instead defaults to the penult (final only if closed)
591.prule: Principal tone (per the Masoretic accentuation) 'as a rule on the final syllable', 'less frequently' on the penultima; never further back. Closure constraints: a closed penult bears the tone only if the ultima is open (qaTAlta, LEKHna); a closed ultima is 'as a rule' toneless only when the penult is open (wayYAqom). Which of final/penult is chosen is otherwise tied to morphology (tone on 'formative additions'; tone moves forward when the word is lengthened, 29c; retracts under waw consecutive, 29d) and to phrasal rhythm (nesiga, 29e-g, where a CVVC ultima never yields the tone and only a CVV penult may receive it). Khan 2020 takes main-stress position as given by the accent signs and states no distributional rule.
591.srule: Secondary stress (the 'counter-tone', marked by Metheg/ga'ya or a conjunctive accent) falls as a rule on the second syllable before the main stress when that syllable is open, on the third when the second is closed (even the fourth when the third is unsuitable), and may recur on the fourth syllable before the tone when it already stands on the second: an alternating pattern leftward from the main stress on open long-vowel syllables, never adjacent to it (GKC 16 c-d, via 29 b). Restated by Khan 2020: 458 - 'a secondary stress falls on a long vowel in an open syllable that is separated from the main stress by at least one other syllable, i.e. there is a eurhythmic alternating sequence'; not on vocalic shewa (pp. 437-438).

592.heavy: Heavy = bimoraic syllable, which in Apurinã means a syllable whose nucleus is a nasal vowel (short OR long) or a diphthong; all other syllables (incl. CV with short oral vowel) are light. Long oral vowels never occur word-finally so are not attested as stress attractors. The language has no codas, so closed syllables play no role.
592.prule: Primary (culminative) stress on the final syllable if it is heavy (nasal vowel or diphthong); otherwise on the penultimate syllable (rule 94 + rule 104). Heavy antepenults do not attract stress. Monosyllables are stressed (and lengthened by a minimal-word requirement). Footnote 8 offers the equivalent restatement 'stress the penultimate mora'.
592.srule: Secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of the primary stress, applied iteratively (rule 96): with the normal penultimate primary, on the 4th, 6th, 8th... syllables from the end, e.g. [ˌtakaˈtarɨ] 'manioc frying pan', [aˌnapaˈnarɨ] 'dog'; not conditioned by syllable weight; analysed as syllabic trochees (2.3.3.3).
592.quote: The most general statement to be made here about stress in the language is that stress is not contrastive. ... the distribution of the highest prominence is largely (if not completely) predictable. [2.3.3.1] the primary stress occurs on word-final syllables when such syllables have a nasal (short or long) vowel or a diphthong. ... 593.heavy: Vowel quality first: /a, e/ are heavy, /i, u, o/ light; syllable closure counts 'to a lesser degree', deciding only when both vowels are of the same quality class (ST1 note: VC > V; VCobs > VCson ?). Long vowels are not named as a weight factor. Schwa/reduced vowels arise in pre-stress position and cannot bear stress.
593.dflt: peninitial (second syllable) when the two vowels are equal in weight, unless closure decides
593.prule: Stress is confined to the first two syllables of the word. The second syllable is stressed if its vowel is not inferior in weight to the first syllable's vowel (weight = vowel quality /a,e/ > /i,u,o/, closure as tiebreaker); otherwise (first vowel heavier) stress is initial. Pre-stress vowels reduce toward schwa.
593.srule: None inside simple (non-compound) words: 'Внутри простого слова не бывает никаких побочных ударений' [no secondary stresses of any kind inside a simple word; a vowel is either fully stressed or unstressed] (Kibrik et al. 1977: 264; likewise Kodzasov 1999 via StressTyp2: underived words show only stressed vs unstressed, 'all unstressed syllables are equally weak'). Secondary stress occurs only in compounds and word + enclitic (postposition, auxiliary) groups, where the first stress is the main one and each following stress is weakened to secondary, e.g. /kʰulú-lò/ 'orphan' (1977: 268).

594.heavy: Bimoraic syllables = long vowels and diphthongs ((C)VV): 'the strongest stress attractor'; Summary point 1: 'All bimoraic syllables have a primary or at least a secondary stress, even final syllables'. (C)VN nasal-closed syllables explicitly do NOT count as heavier than (C)V (Summary point 4, contra J. Payne 1991 and Crowhurst & Michael 2005 for sister varieties). Additional gradient factors: vowel quality ('/a/-syllables are the heaviest and /i/-syllables the weakest', point 7) and, in longer words only, a coda /ʃ/ or /ʦʰ/ created by /i/-deletion 'appears to attract stress' (point 11).
594.dflt: 1st syllable in disyllables, 2nd syllable in 3-6-syllable words (final syllable extrametrical, iambs from the left; secondary on 4th in 5-6-syllable words)
594.prule: Default (words of 2-4 syllables, no bimoraic syllable): final syllable extrametrical, iambic feet from the left, so stress on the 1st syllable of disyllables and on the 2nd syllable of tri- and tetrasyllables (= penult in 2-3-syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable words). A bimoraic (CVV) syllable anywhere in the word attracts the stress instead, even onto a final syllable (rowáe, otháwinatakàe). Vowel quality (/a/ attracts, /i/ repels), word-initial /ɾ/ (< *iɾ-) and some morphemes further perturb placement. Author states these are tendencies, not rigid rules; placement varies across tokens (méyiri ~ meiri ~ meirí) and between narrative and dictation (19 of 163 words).
594.srule: 5- and 6-syllable words with no bimoraic syllable: secondary stress on the 4th syllable (primary on the 2nd; iambic feet L->R, final syllable extrametrical). Every bimoraic syllable bears a primary or at least a secondary stress, even word-finally; a heavy-syllable primary can force a secondary onto an otherwise unstressed initial foot ('disyllabic feet tend to be stressed', weaker in long words); some 4-syllable words with a bimoraic 1st syllable have a secondary on the 3rd (káakitàki). Enclitics (demonstrative =ra, =rika, =ki, =paeni, =wee) and possessive -ti/-ni tend to carry a secondary stress. In words of 7+ syllables the iterative iambic pattern 'does not operate' (only two stresses in 7-8-syllable words, three in 9-10); there a second stress tends to fall immediately before the 3rd-person object suffix -ri/-ro. Primary vs secondary distinguished by ear and 'tentative' (fn. 33).

599.heavy: CVV = bimoraic (heavy): 'Banawá syllables are maximally bimoraic' (16); only CV and CVV syllables, no V-syllables, no codas; every vowel maps to a mora ((18) 'Max Vµ: [-cons] segments correspond to moras'); 'Banawá diphthongs are all bimoraic' (p.40), so both falling (kei, ai) and rising (ia, ua) CVV sequences count two moras (fúa.nà = (µµ)(µ), sú.kià = (µµ)(µ)); long/geminate vowels only in bimoraic monosyllables (fáa, bíi). The 'rising diphthongs monomoraic' (RISDIPH) analysis in the paper applies to Suruwahá (sec. 5), not Banawá.
599.dflt: all-CV words: stress every odd-numbered mora counting from the first footable vowel (initial onsetless vowel skipped in words of >2 syllables; bimoraic V-initial words stress the initial vowel: ába, úwi); primary per Everett 1996's marks on the penultimate foot head = first/peninitial syllable in words of up to two feet (wárabù, wánakàri, uwárià), medial in three-foot words
599.prule: Feet: left-to-right moraic trochees over the word (FTBIN on moras, ALIGN FT (FT, L, PRWD, L), left-headed), CVV = two moras and feet may split a CVV syllable (SYLLINT violated), a word-initial onsetless vowel is left unfooted in words of more than two syllables, and a word-final degenerate (monomoraic) foot is built when the footable mora count is odd. Which foot carries PRIMARY stress is not stated as a rule in Everett 1996; his diacritics (´ primary, ` secondary) put the acute on the head of the penultimate foot: the first foot in two-foot words (wánakàri, dábikàri, súkià, fúanà, enémedè, mákarì) but the medial foot in three-foot words (kèiyárinè (40a), kèrewéduàma (83a), tìkadámuèi (84a)), and p.30 says degenerate (final) feet are not 'where primary stress falls'. Two forms are also cited with final primary (màkarí p.32 vs mákarì (69e)/(80); kàwarìe-í ~ káwarìe-i (45c)), the Everett-1995 final-foot pattern that StressTyp2/WALS adopted. Either way primary position is fixed by the mora count from the left edge.
599.srule: All other foot heads carry secondary stress: every other mora L->R from the first footable vowel; the word-final degenerate (monomoraic) foot is stressed in words with an odd number of footable moras (súkià, mákarì, afíyamà); because feet may split a CVV syllable the surface pattern equals 'stress every other vowel, skip initial vowels' (StressTyp2 passage). Word-final post-vocalic high vowels never bear stress (43g).

variants.prule: Stress falls on the syllable containing the penultimate mora of the phonological word (short vowel = 1 mora, long vowel = 2 moras), and on the syllables containing every second mora leftward from it (2nd, 4th, 6th... moras from the end). Syllables are (C)V, so in an all-short-vowel word this is the penultimate syllable (hósi, kobája) and in a word ending in a long vowel it is the final syllable (which holds the 1st…
variants.quote: Jarawara has just four vowels (i, e, a and o) with contrastive length ... Syllable structure is (C)V. The stress rule operates in terms of moras, with a short vowel counting as one mora and a long vowel as two moras. Now in the related Banawá dialect, stress goes on syllables including the first, third, etc. moras from the beginning of the word, ignoring a word-initial V in a word with three or more moras (see Buller, Buller and Everett 1993); the Jamamadí dialect has a similar rule. It is likely that this was the stress rule at an earlier stage of Jarawara. However, Jarawara now has penultimate assignment – stress goes on syllables including the second, fourth, etc. moras from the end of the word. It will be seen that in a word with an even number of moras the stress rule is the same in all dialects, e.g. hósi ‘sweet potato’. However, in a word with an odd-number of moras, stress goes on odd-numbered moras in Banawá and Jamamadí, e.g. kóbajá ‘white-collared peccary’, but on even-numbered moras in Jarawara – kobája. ... The criteria for phonological word in Jarawara are: (a) A phonological word must include at least two moras. Thus, if it is monosyllabic the vowel must be long. (b) The stress rule operates within a phonological word.

603.heavy: Light (stress-repelling) = an OPEN penultimate syllable containing /ə/; all other penults (any full vowel, open or closed, and CLOSED syllables with /ə/, e.g. [jə́lma] 'person', [pə́ʔpəʔ] 'hit') keep penultimate stress. 604.dq: Wedekind et al. 2008 <27>: 'Every Beja word will have at least one syllable which is louder and which has a higher pitch than the other(s). The louder syllable is said to carry the pitch-accent'; Almkvist §47: 'Hat das Wort nur einen Accent, so kann er nicht vor der Antepenultima stehen'.
604.dloc: Wedekind, Wedekind & Musa 2008, 'Suprasegmentals: Pitch Accent' <27>; Almkvist 1881, III 'Der Accent' §47, p.57
604.heavy: Almkvist 1881: a penult that is 'lang oder geschlossen' (long vowel or closed) takes/keeps the accent; for the ultima of disyllables only vowel length counts (short-vowel ultima, open or closed, leaves accent on penult; long ultima draws it off a short open penult but not off a closed one). Wedekind et al. 2008: NO weight criterion at all -- accent is an inherent property of each morpheme/root, the last accent in the word surfaces, plurals front-shift it.
604.dflt: Almkvist: antepenult in trisyllables, penult in disyllables (never before the antepenult); Wedekind et al.: not applicable -- position is lexical (inherent accent of the last accented morpheme)
604.prule: CONFLICT. Almkvist 1881 (Bishari, self-declared provisional §40): disyllables accent penult 'in der Mehrzahl der Fälle' (always if ultima short-vowelled), ultima 'im allgemeinen' if long and penult short-open, closed penult keeps accent; trisyllables antepenult 'im allgemeinen' unless penult long or closed (then penult); single accent never before the antepenult (§47); plus morphological attraction (§44-45). Wedekind, Wedekind & Musa 2008 (all dialects): pitch-accent; 'Every morpheme or word root has its inherent accent... part of the root in the same way as the meaning, the gender, or the consonants and vowels'; in polymorphemic words '(only) the last accent will be articulated'; plurals shift the accent one syllable toward the beginning (not in Bishaari). No weight-based placement rule in the modern description.
604.srule: Almkvist 1881 (Bishari) only: words of three or more syllables 'sehr oft' carry two or more accents, 'meistens... fonetisch als gleichgestellt' (main vs secondary only etymologically); the extra accents he places are morphological -- the prefixed article is always accented while the noun keeps its own accent (§43), the 2PL ending -ána and the verbal endings -tána/-ána/-tenia take an accent beside the stem accent (§§44-45) -- plus an unformulated 'durchaus rytmisches Tongesetz' in longer forms (§46). Wedekind, Wedekind & Musa 2008 describe no secondary accent ('(only) the last accent will be articulated', <45>); Hudson 1973/1974 likewise allow more than one accent per word, one per morphological accent-unit, unranked; Vanhove 2014 §2.4 does not mention secondary stress.
604.quote: ... contrary to the claims of Reinisch (1893: 55) (cf. also Almkvist, 1881: 57), a single word may contain more than one accented syllable ... since the unit of distribution for accents is the accent-unit, not the word ... the later of two inherent accents in the same accent-unit is realized. 604.idn: The two cited sources describe different Beja dialects: Almkvist 1881 the Bischari (Bishari, northern) dialect, Wedekind et al. 2008 the Atman variety of Port Sudan and Suakin; Wedekind (<40> item 10, <45> rule 3) states that Bishaari lacks the plural accent front-shift, so part of the disagreement may be dialectal…

Dagegen wird im allgemeinen die letzte Silbe betont'; §40: rules 'dürften ... vielfach ergänzt und modifizirt werden'; Wedekind <45>: 'Every morpheme or word root has its inherent accent.'
604.tone: Wedekind, Wedekind & Musa 2008 treat Beja word prominence under 'Suprasegmentals: Pitch Accent': the accented syllable is 'louder... has a higher pitch', one per word at least, inherent to each root/morpheme with only the last articulated; sentence intonation (falling/rising on 'the last stressed syllable') is described separately. undet.detail: pitch-accent (Hudson 1973: 'not a tone-language... but has a pitch-accent system'; Wedekind et al. 2008 'pitch-accent'; Vanhove 2025 'pitch accent'; Vanhove 2020: 'no phonological tones'). Placement is lexical-morphological, not weight-computed: every root/morpheme carries (or lacks) an inherent accent of type 'final' or 'penultimate' relative to a reference-point in its last syllable…

tones: penultimate accent (on the syllable—or mora—before the reference-point)
tn.quote: The accent system basically involves simply a distinction between accented and unaccented syllables, where ' accent ' is realized phonetically as a relatively high pitch. However ... a single word may contain more than one accented syllable ..., since the unit of distribution for accents is the accent-unit, not the word ... A morpheme may or may not have an inherent accent, but if it does, there are two further variables to be specified ... allowing us to speak of final accent (on the reference-point itself) and penultimate accent (on the syllable—or mora—before the reference-point).
tn.cite: Hudson, R. A. (1974). A structural sketch of Beja. African Language Studies 15: 111-142.
tn.note: Pitch accent, 'not a tone-language' (1973): morphemes have or lack an inherent final or penultimate accent = high pitch on a mora, one per accent-unit; falling only on long syllables; question accent.

604.cfw: Hudson 1973-1976, Wedekind, Wedekind & Musa 2008 and Vanhove 2014 all describe a lexical-morphological pitch accent whose position within the last three syllables is not predictable from syllable weight, against the quantity-based rules of Almkvist 1881 and Reinisch 1893, which both authors themselves called provisional, and a passing line in Vanhove 2020 that stress 'mostly depends on the syllabic structure', while Vanhove's 2017 reference grammar has not been consulted.

ev.text: In a phrase, which of course may consist of a single word, only the last word is accented. Accent is thus a property of phrases rather than of words, but word boundaries and the internal phonological structure of words determine in the following manner the syllabic element on which the accent falls.
